fixes.explanation: Mark says it right in the verse: Preparation Day is "…the day before the Sabbath…" So it was already evening, and the Sabbath was close. Joseph of Arimathea, a Council member, is about to act on that same evening.

Mark says Joseph of Arimathea "…boldly went to Pilate…" He's walking up to ask for the body of a man who was crucified. I think that takes nerve. I'd rehearse that walk all the way there and still open with a comment about the weather.

Pilate doesn't call for the high priest here. The text says he summons the centurion to ask if Jesus is already dead. Pilate was surprised to hear it, and I think he wanted his answer from the centurion. Once Pilate confirmed it with him, he granted the body to Joseph.

A tetrarch is a ruler over a part of a region, and Luke 3:1 names Herod as tetrarch of Galilee. But Pilate doesn't summon one in this scene. Mark says he summons the centurion to ask if Jesus is already dead. The Bible has plenty of titles, friend, and I'd have panicked at them too.
No oak tree in this scene, friend. Mark says Joseph placed the body in a tomb that had been cut out of the rock. Then he rolled a stone against the entrance. The text doesn't mention any tree.
Joseph rolled a stone against the entrance to the tomb. Later, Mark tells us this stone was extremely large (Mark 16:4). Keep that in mind, friend. It comes up again when the women get there.
Mark doesn't mention a log. The text says Joseph rolled a stone against the entrance. Later it calls that stone extremely large (Mark 16:4). The women will ask about that stone.
Mary Magdalene and Mary the mother of Joseph saw where His body was placed. They're looking right at the spot. I think that's a heavy moment, and they're there for it.
They bought spices so they could go and anoint the body of Jesus. Mark says they bought them when the Sabbath was over. I think those spices tell us what they expect to find: the body of Jesus.
Guarding isn't what the spices are for. Mark says they bought them so they could go and anoint the body of Jesus. Spices are for anointing, friend. Nobody ever guarded anything with a bag of spices.

They were asking one another, "Who will roll away the stone from the entrance of the tomb?" They're thinking about a very big stone. Mark records the question, and I think they're working through the problem as they go.

Mark doesn't record the women asking about soldiers. They ask, "Who will roll away the stone from the entrance of the tomb?" I think that's a practical worry about getting inside. The text doesn't mention soldiers anywhere near here.

Mary Magdalene, one of the women headed there, saw where His body was placed (Mark 15:47). So I think their question isn't about which tomb. It's about the stone: "Who will roll away the stone from the entrance of the tomb?"
It's the opposite. Mark says that when they looked up, the stone had been rolled away. It was extremely large, and it was moved anyway. The stone they were asking about was already rolled away.
They entered the tomb and saw a young man dressed in a white robe, sitting on the right side. Mark doesn't give his name. So I'll call him what the text calls him: a young man.

Joseph's linen was the cloth he bought to wrap the body (Mark 15:46). He isn't sitting in the tomb. The women see a young man dressed in a white robe, on the right side. Joseph's part came earlier, friend.
Mark doesn't say relieved. He says they were alarmed. Then the young man tells them, "Do not be alarmed."
Mark says that when the women saw him, they were alarmed, not delighted. Then the young man says, "Do not be alarmed." After that he gives them the news: "He has risen!"
The young man says, "He has risen! He is not here!" Then he tells them, "See the place where they put Him." The tomb is empty because Jesus has risen. That's the heart of this whole passage.
He doesn't say that. The young man says, "He has risen! He is not here!" Moving Jesus to another tomb isn't in his words. He says Jesus has risen.
The message says, "He is going ahead of you into Galilee." The young man adds, "There you will see Him…" The disciples are given a place to go.
Emmaus is a village that shows up in Luke 24:13. It isn't in the message here. The young man says Jesus is going ahead of the disciples into Galilee. Different destination, friend.
Mark says the opposite. In their fear they did not say a word to anyone. They left the tomb and ran away, trembling and bewildered. Nobody heard anything from them.
